scenes.title: FULL JOIN
scenes.narration: A FULL JOIN returns every row from both tables, filling in NULLs wherever a match is missing on either side.

scenes.title: What FULL JOIN returns
bullets: All matched rows, combining both tables.
All unmatched left rows, with NULLs on the right.
All unmatched right rows, with NULLs on the left.
scenes.narration: It returns the matched rows just like an inner join would. It also returns unmatched left rows with NULLs on the right, and unmatched right rows with NULLs on the left. In effect it is the union of a left join and a right join.

scenes.title: Reconciling two datasets
scenes.code:
SELECT COALESCE(a.id, b.id) AS id,
       a.amount AS ledger_amount,
       b.amount AS bank_amount
FROM ledger AS a
FULL JOIN bank AS b
  ON a.id = b.id;
scenes.narration: This reconciles a ledger against bank records, showing every id that appears in either source. Matched ids show both amounts side by side, while an id present in only one table shows NULL for the missing side. COALESCE picks whichever id is present so the key column is never NULL.

scenes.title: Finding the mismatches
steps: FULL JOIN both tables on the key.
Rows where one side is NULL are unmatched.
Add WHERE a.id IS NULL OR b.id IS NULL.
You now see only the discrepancies.
scenes.narration: To surface only the discrepancies between two datasets, full join them and then keep the rows where either key is NULL. Those NULLs mark records that exist in one source but not the other, which is exactly what a reconciliation report needs.

scenes.title: FULL JOIN vs INNER JOIN
scenes.narration: A full join shows the complete picture including everything that failed to match on either side, using NULLs to flag the gaps. An inner join shows only the overlap and silently hides the rest. Reach for full join when the unmatched records themselves are the point.

scenes.title: Emulating FULL JOIN in MySQL
scenes.code:
SELECT a.id, a.amount, b.amount
FROM ledger AS a
LEFT JOIN bank AS b ON a.id = b.id
UNION
SELECT b.id, a.amount, b.amount
FROM ledger AS a
RIGHT JOIN bank AS b ON a.id = b.id;
scenes.narration: MySQL does not support FULL JOIN directly, so you emulate it by combining a left join and a right join with UNION. The left join contributes all left rows plus matches, the right join contributes all right rows plus matches, and UNION removes the duplicate matched rows. The result is equivalent to a true full outer join.

scenes.text: FULL JOIN shines for reconciliation: comparing two sources to find records present in one but missing from the other.
scenes.narration: Full join is ideal for reconciliation work, where you must compare two sources and spot records missing from either one.
